title: Why Ordinary Regression Fails for Time-to-Event Data

blocks.label: Definition
blocks.html: Time-to-event data cannot be analysed by ordinary linear regression on the time, or logistic regression on whether the event happened, when some subjects are censored: their follow-up ends before the event, so their true event time is known only to exceed their observed time.

blocks.label: Simplified Explanation
blocks.html: A “time until dropout” looks like a continuous outcome for linear regression. The problem is the subjects who have not dropped out when the study ends. Their true time is longer than what you saw, but you do not know by how much. Excluding them wastes real information and biases the sample towards early events. Treating their last observed time as their event time shortens every one of their times. Neither is valid.

blocks.label: Illustration / Example
blocks.html: Take a conceptual study (not the §14.7 cohort) that follows 100 CBHI members for 3 years. Some drop out during the study; their dropout time is known. Others are still enrolled at 3 years. For them, “3 years” is not a dropout time: many would have stayed enrolled much longer had the study continued. Entering 3 years as their outcome in a regression would understate how long members typically stay.

points.html: Dropping censored subjects is a selection problem: those left in the analysis are no longer like the cohort that started (§17.2.1 treats selection bias). A censored subject’s event-free time up to the last contact is genuine, usable data.
Treating a censoring time as an event time biases the average time to event downwards.
Survival methods use each subject’s data exactly up to the point where it is known, and no further.
Poisson regression with log person-time as the offset (recall §13.4) also uses censored follow-up correctly, but it assumes a constant rate over the follow-up. Survival methods drop that assumption.
